stem: An organisation's retention schedule requires customer transaction records to be kept for seven years. Records from twelve years ago are still held in production. What is the correct characterisation?

options.text: A disposal failure, not a retention success
options.why: A retention schedule sets a ceiling as well as a floor. Data held beyond its retention period is liability without benefit, still discoverable and still breachable, which is why disposal is a named activity.

options.text: Good practice, since keeping more history is always safer
options.why: This instinct is exactly what disposal rules exist to correct. Every extra year is more data to lose and more to produce in discovery.

options.text: A legal hold, since the records are still being preserved
options.why: A hold is a deliberate instruction to preserve specific material for litigation. Forgetting to delete is not one.

options.text: A classification error on the old records
options.why: Nothing suggests the records were classified wrongly; they were simply never disposed of.

stem: Litigation begins. Automated deletion under the retention schedule would remove email relevant to the case next week. What must happen?

options.text: A legal hold must suspend scheduled deletion of the relevant material
options.why: A hold overrides routine disposal. Letting automation delete relevant material once litigation is anticipated is spoliation, regardless of the schedule being followed.

options.text: The retention schedule takes precedence, since it is documented policy
options.why: Preservation obligations override internal schedules. The schedule being documented does not excuse the destruction.

options.text: The material should be sanitized rather than simply deleted
options.why: Both destroy the evidence. The requirement is to keep it.

options.text: The retention period should be permanently extended for all email
options.why: A hold is scoped to relevant material and lifted when the matter ends. Extending everything forever recreates the liability problem.

stem: An asset register lists four hundred servers, of which sixty have no named owner. Why does this matter beyond administrative tidiness?

options.text: Nobody is accountable for patching, classification or changes
options.why: Ownership is the hook every other control hangs on. An unowned asset has nobody to chase, nobody to approve its changes and nobody answering for its state, so it drifts out of every other process.

options.text: The register cannot be exported for audit without complete fields
options.why: A formatting concern. The substantive risk is that nothing happens to those servers.

options.text: Unowned assets are automatically classified as public
options.why: No such default exists, and that would be a worse outcome than having no classification.

options.text: Ownership is only required for data, not for hardware like servers
options.why: Ownership applies across hardware, software and data.

stem: A server was replaced two years ago. The replacement went live, but the original was left powered on and is still reachable, unpatched and unmonitored. Which activity was incomplete?

options.text: Decommissioning of the original server
options.why: Decommissioning is an activity with steps: retiring an asset means removing it from service, from the network and from the inventory, not just ceasing to use it. A host nobody uses and nobody patches is among the most attractive things on a network.

options.text: Sanitization of the server's media before disposal
options.why: That applies when the hardware leaves. The problem here is that it never left and is still running.

options.text: Classification of the data the original server held
options.why: Would not have changed the outcome; the host would still be live.

options.text: Certification of destruction for the old hardware
options.why: Certification evidences destruction that has happened. Nothing was destroyed.

stem: A disposal vendor collects two hundred decommissioned drives and shreds them. What does the organisation still require to discharge its obligation?

options.text: A certificate of destruction listing the specific media
options.why: Certification is the documented evidence. Without it you cannot demonstrate the obligation was met, and in an audit or a breach investigation an undocumented destruction is indistinguishable from none.

options.text: Nothing further, since the drives are physically destroyed
options.why: Having done the work and being able to show it are different, and only one of them survives scrutiny.

options.text: A sanitisation report, since shredding is a form of sanitisation
options.why: Sanitisation makes media reusable by removing data. Shredding is destruction, and the artefact is a destruction certificate.

options.text: Confirmation that the drives were encrypted before collection
options.why: Sound practice and not the required evidence of disposal.

stem: Why is acquisition and procurement treated as part of asset management rather than as a purely finance process?

options.text: Because an asset enters the inventory and gains an owner at that point
options.why: Procurement is where an asset becomes known: it gains an owner and a classification, and inherits security requirements. Anything bought outside it is shadow IT: unowned, uninventoried and outside every control that depends on the register.

options.text: Because security must approve every purchase before it is made
options.why: Overstates it. The point is that the asset is recorded and assigned, not that security holds a veto on spend.

options.text: Because procurement sets the retention period for the data it will hold
options.why: Retention is driven by the data and its legal regime, not by how the hardware was bought.

options.text: Because acquisition is when sanitisation requirements are applied
options.why: Sanitisation happens at end of life.

stem: What is the relationship between enumeration and inventory in asset management?

options.text: Enumeration discovers what exists; the inventory is the record
options.why: Discovery finds reality, the inventory states what you believe, and the gap between them is what asset management works to close. Devices present in enumeration and absent from inventory are exactly the unmanaged assets worth worrying about.

options.text: They are the same activity under two different names
options.why: One is an act of discovery, the other a record. They disagree constantly, which is the point of comparing them.

options.text: Enumeration applies to software and inventory to hardware
options.why: Both apply across hardware, software and data.

options.text: Inventory is produced by the procurement system and needs no enumeration
options.why: Procurement captures what was bought through the process. Enumeration catches everything else.

stem: Which TWO statements about data retention and disposal are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: A retention schedule sets both a keep period and a disposal point
options.why: A floor and a ceiling: a minimum keep period and a point at which data must be disposed of. Only treating it as a floor is what produces twelve-year-old records in production.

options.text: A legal hold suspends scheduled deletion for the material it covers
options.why: Preservation obligations override routine disposal, and automated deletion continuing during litigation is spoliation.

options.text: Keeping data indefinitely is the safest default for compliance
options.why: It is accumulating liability: more to breach, more to produce in discovery, more to secure.

options.text: Destruction and sanitisation are interchangeable terms
options.why: Sanitisation removes data so media can be reused; destruction makes the media unusable.

options.text: Certification is optional where destruction was witnessed internally
options.why: The documented record is what demonstrates the obligation was met.

stem: A vulnerability programme repeatedly misses hosts. Investigation finds devices in service that appear in no asset register. What is the root problem?

options.text: Asset inventory and tracking gaps
options.why: Asset management sits underneath vulnerability management. An incomplete inventory caps how good scanning can ever be. You cannot scan or patch what you do not know exists.

options.text: The scanner's configuration and plugin set
options.why: The scanner covered what it was told about. The gap is what it was never told about.

options.text: The patch management cadence for servers
options.why: Cadence governs how fast known hosts are patched. These hosts are not known.

options.text: Insufficient network segmentation
options.why: Segmentation limits movement. It neither finds nor registers unknown devices.

stem: Laptops coming off a three year lease must be returned to the leasing company. What is the correct disposal control?

options.text: Sanitization, backed by a certificate
options.why: The devices are being reused by someone else, so they must be wiped rather than destroyed, and the certificate recording it is the evidence an auditor will ask for. Reused by someone else: sanitize. Never reused: destroy.

options.text: Physical destruction of the drives before return
options.why: Destroying drives in leased equipment you must return intact is both a contract problem and unnecessary.

options.text: Deleting the user profiles and reformatting
options.why: Formatting leaves data recoverable. It is not a sanitization method.

options.text: Degaussing each device before return
options.why: Degaussing destroys magnetic media and does nothing to an SSD, which stores no magnetic domains. It also destroys the drive you must return.

stem: A dispute arises over whether a dataset may be shared with a partner, and nobody can say who decides. Which asset management practice was missing?

options.text: Assigning a named owner to the dataset
options.why: Every asset needs a named owner who is accountable for classification and access decisions, with a classification attached. Without one, questions like this have no answer. Who decides? The owner.

options.text: Enumeration of the asset in the inventory
options.why: Knowing it exists is necessary and does not say who decides about it.

options.text: A data retention schedule for the dataset
options.why: Retention governs how long it is kept, not who may share it.

options.text: Secure disposal procedures for the dataset
options.why: Disposal is the end of the lifecycle and is not in play.

stem: At which point in the asset lifecycle should security requirements first be applied?

options.text: Acquisition and procurement, before purchase
options.why: Requirements set before the purchase is made prevent acquiring something that can never meet policy. Afterwards you are negotiating with a contract already signed. Security belongs in the purchase, not after it.

options.text: At deployment, once the device is on the network
options.why: By then you own something that may be incapable of meeting the standard.

options.text: At the first vulnerability scan after deployment
options.why: Far too late, and scanning only reports what is already true.

options.text: At decommissioning, when the device is retired
options.why: That is the end of the lifecycle.

stem: A failed SSD held regulated data and cannot be wiped because it no longer responds. What is the correct disposal route?

options.text: Physical destruction, with a certificate of destruction
options.why: Sanitization requires a working device. When the media has failed, destruction is the only route that guarantees the data is gone, and the certificate is the evidence.

options.text: Degaussing the drive with an approved degausser
options.why: Degaussing erases magnetic domains. An SSD stores charge in flash cells and is completely unaffected by it.

options.text: Overwriting every sector three times
options.why: Overwriting is a sanitization method and it needs a drive that responds to writes. This one does not.

options.text: Returning it to the vendor under warranty without further action
options.why: That hands regulated data to a third party. Warranty returns of storage holding sensitive data normally need a destruction clause or a retain-the-drive agreement.

stem: A retention schedule says finance records are deleted after seven years. The company receives a litigation hold notice covering one set of 2017 invoices that are now eight years old. What should happen to those invoices?

options.text: Preserve them until the hold is lifted
options.why: A legal hold overrides the schedule. Deleting hold material can be treated as spoliation of evidence.

options.text: Delete them, because the schedule is the approved policy
options.why: The schedule is overridden for anything under a hold. Following it here would destroy evidence.

options.text: Sanitize them and keep the media
options.why: Sanitization is how data is removed. The point is that these records must not be removed yet.

options.text: Move them to a cheaper tier and let automated deletion continue
options.why: Moving them changes nothing about automated deletion. Deletion jobs must be suspended for held data.

stem: A network scan lists 1,150 live devices. The asset register lists 1,000. What is the right reading?

options.text: 150 devices are unaccounted for and need identifying
options.why: Enumeration finds what is really there. Comparing it with the inventory exposes unmanaged or unrecorded assets, which must be identified and then added to the register or removed.

options.text: The register is correct and the scan is over-counting
options.why: The register is a record and can go stale. A live scan is evidence of what exists.

options.text: Nothing, because inventory and enumeration are the same activity
options.why: Enumeration discovers assets; inventory is the maintained record. The gap between them is the finding.

options.text: The 150 extra devices are ones already disposed of
options.why: A disposed device is no longer on the network. These are responding, so they are live.

stem: A hospital will resell used laptops and wants the drives reused safely. Which approach fits, and what proves it was done?

options.text: Sanitize with an approved wipe and keep the certificate
options.why: Sanitization removes data so the media can be reused. The certificate of sanitization is the audit evidence. Reuse means sanitize, no reuse means destroy.

options.text: Shred the drives and keep the certificate of destruction
options.why: Shredding destroys the media, so nothing can be resold.

options.text: Delete the files and empty the recycle bin
options.why: Deletion removes only references. The data stays recoverable.

options.text: Keep the drives in storage until the retention period ends
options.why: Retention concerns the records, not the media. The laptops are leaving, so the data must be removed.

stem: A new SaaS product is adopted by one department. Months later security finds it holds customer data and has no named owner. Which lifecycle activity was most clearly skipped?

options.text: Assigning ownership at acquisition
options.why: Ownership and accountability are set at acquisition so someone is responsible for the asset's risk and its disposal. No owner at purchase means nobody owns the risk later.

options.text: Disposal and decommissioning of the product
options.why: Disposal is the final stage. The product is still in use.

options.text: Data sanitization of the customer records
options.why: Sanitization applies at end of life, not here.

options.text: Applying the retention schedule to its data
options.why: Retention matters, but nobody can apply it until an owner exists.

stem: A company is closing a cloud storage account that held regulated data in volumes it encrypted with its own keys. It cannot witness the provider destroy any disks. Which disposal approach fits?

options.text: Ask the provider for a certificate that the disks were shredded
options.why: The provider's physical destruction cannot be witnessed or controlled by the customer.

options.text: Destroy the encryption keys, and record that it was done
options.why: Cryptographic erase sanitizes data the customer owns when the customer controls the keys, leaving the data unreadable. Keeping a record supports the proof. You cannot shred their disks, but you can destroy your keys.

options.text: Delete the files, then delete the account and the storage volumes
options.why: Deleting removes pointers. Without more, the data can remain on disk.

options.text: Degauss the cloud storage volumes with an approved degausser
options.why: Degaussing is a physical process for magnetic media. It cannot be done to a cloud volume.

stem: A storage room holds retired magnetic hard drives and backup tapes that held confidential records. Which TWO methods fully remove the data? (Choose two.)

options.text: Quick formatting each drive before storage
options.why: A quick format rewrites the file system structures. The data remains readable with ordinary tools.

options.text: Degaussing with an approved degausser
options.why: A strong magnetic field destroys the recorded pattern on magnetic media, whether disk or tape.

options.text: Deleting the files and emptying the recycle bin
options.why: Deletion frees space and leaves the content behind.

options.text: Shredding or pulverizing the media
options.why: Physical destruction, done in house or by a destruction vendor, is the surest method when the media will never be reused. Never reused: destroy.

options.text: Moving the drives and tapes to a locked cabinet
options.why: Storing them is not sanitizing them. The data is still on them.

stem: Two groups of drives are due for disposal: drives from the legal department that held privileged case files, and drives from a lobby information kiosk that held only public content. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Both groups must be shredded, because any drive could still hold sensitive data
options.why: Over treating public media wastes money and loses reusable assets. Method follows what the media held.

options.text: Classification stops applying once a drive has been powered off and removed
options.why: Classification travels with the data on the media until it is properly sanitized or destroyed.

options.text: Wipe and reuse the kiosk drives; destroy or purge the legal drives
options.why: Method follows classification. The more sensitive the data, the stronger the method and the proof: legal drives need destruction or a verified purge, while public media can be reused after a basic wipe.

options.text: A single standard wipe is enough for both groups, as it is for any drive
options.why: A basic wipe fits the kiosk drives. It is not adequate for the most sensitive material.

stem: The owner of a set of finance servers and the data on them has left the company. Their name is still on every record. What should happen first?

options.text: Decommission the servers immediately because nobody owns them now
options.why: Retiring assets because the owner left is not a decision. It would destroy live business data.

options.text: Leave the record unchanged until the next scheduled annual audit review
options.why: Without an owner nobody can approve access, patches or retirement in the meantime.

options.text: Assign a new accountable owner and update the asset record
options.why: Every asset needs a named owner at all times. Ownership transfers with offboarding, before access and decisions are left orphaned.

options.text: Make IT operations the owner of all the data held on them
options.why: Operating a system is not owning the data. The business must decide who may use it.

stem: A server is being decommissioned. Which TWO actions belong in the process? (Choose two.)

options.text: Sanitize or destroy its storage before it leaves your control
options.why: Media is the last place data survives. Disposal is not complete until it is dealt with.

options.text: Leave its accounts and certificates active in case it is needed again
options.why: A decommissioned asset's credentials are a standing risk. They should be revoked.

options.text: Mark it retired in the inventory and remove it from monitoring
options.why: A retired asset that stays on the register hides gaps, and monitoring a machine that is gone creates noise. Retired means retired everywhere: register, monitoring and network.

options.text: Sell it with its drives in place after deleting the user accounts
options.why: Deleting accounts leaves the data on the drives. Selling it like that is a disclosure.

options.text: Keep it powered on in a spare rack for a year, just in case
options.why: An unmanaged powered asset is how a forgotten, unpatched machine appears.

stem: An asset inventory shows that forty servers run an operating system whose vendor support ends in three months. What is the right use of this information?

options.text: Plan upgrades or replacement now, prioritized by importance
options.why: Tracking lifecycle dates is a security use of inventory. It turns a future gap into a scheduled change, made before patches stop and ordered by each server's importance.

options.text: Wait until support has ended and then decide what to do about it
options.why: By then the servers stop receiving patches. The warning period is the time to act.

options.text: Assume the vendor will extend support for these servers at no cost
options.why: Extensions are not guaranteed, and rarely free.

options.text: Remove the servers from the inventory because they are old
options.why: A system left running but not tracked is how an unpatched one becomes a surprise.

stem: Procurement finds the same network switches advertised at far below the manufacturer's price by a reseller that is not an authorized partner. What is the main security concern?

options.text: The warranty period may be shorter than with an authorized partner
options.why: It may be, but it is not the main security concern.

options.text: There is no concern provided the devices power on and pass a basic test
options.why: A device can work and still carry a modified firmware or counterfeit parts.

options.text: There is no concern if the invoice and warranty paperwork look genuine
options.why: Paperwork is as easy to fake as the hardware. It does not prove where the devices came from or that they are untampered.

options.text: The devices may be counterfeit or tampered with
options.why: A compromised device in the network is harder to find than one bought from a trusted source, so buy from authorized channels and check provenance. Acquisition is where trust begins.

stem: A destruction vendor's certificate states that 200 drives were shredded. The company's asset records show 212 drives retired for that collection. What is the right response?

options.text: Treat the twelve drives as unaccounted for and investigate custody
options.why: Evidence of destruction has to match the inventory serial for serial, so reconcile serial numbers with the manifest and certificate. A gap is a possible data loss until proven otherwise.

options.text: Accept the certificate, since the vendor is a certified destruction company
options.why: A certificate that does not match the records does not discharge the obligation, whoever issued it.

options.text: Ask the vendor to reissue the certificate showing 212 drives and file it
options.why: Changing the paperwork does not show what happened to the other drives.

options.text: Record the difference as a normal handling loss and close the collection
options.why: Drives holding data are not an acceptable loss. They are potential exposure.
